name: Claw machine business
blurb: Place claw and crane machines in busy spots, stock prizes and split takings with the host
title: Claw Machine Business: How It Works, Rules and Risks
description: How a claw machine or small arcade business makes money, the prize and gaming rules to check, who it suits, the main risks and how to test a spot first.
h1: How to start a claw machine business
answer: A claw machine business places crane games in shops, malls, restaurants or a small arcade and earns what players pay per try, minus the cost of prizes and the host's share. Locations and prize choice drive everything, and in some places claw machines fall under gambling or amusement-game rules, so the legal check comes before the first purchase.

sections.h: How a claw machine makes money
body: Players pay per try by coin, token, card or app. Out of the takings you pay for prizes, the location host (usually a share of revenue or a fixed rent), card-reader or app fees, repairs and your time servicing the machine.

Most machines let the operator adjust claw strength or payout, and that is where legal and reputational risk sits. Players who feel a machine is rigged stop playing and complain online, and some regulators set rules on how often a machine must pay out or how much prizes can be worth. A small arcade spot with several machines works the same way, with more rent and more upkeep.

ul: One or more machines, new or used. Check that spare parts exist and that the machine can take cards if your area has moved away from cash.
A written location agreement covering revenue split, power, notice period and who handles breakdowns.
A steady supply of prizes that people actually want, bought wholesale, with safety marks where toys are sold to children.

Local rules: they differ widely. Some places treat crane games as amusement devices needing a licence or permit per machine, some cap prize values, and some have restricted or banned them as gambling. Check with your local authority before buying.
Business registration, public liability insurance and a way to track takings per machine.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who enjoy tinkering with machines and running a route
Operators with access to busy family or youth venues
Places where crane games are restricted or unclear legally
People who track numbers and rotate prizes often
Anyone uncomfortable explaining payout settings to a regulator

ul: Legal grey areas: whether a claw machine is a game of skill or of chance is decided locally. In parts of Canada, for example, single-play cranes have been treated as games of chance.
Payout settings: setting the claw too weak can break local rules and kill repeat play.
Machine sellers promising locations and fixed returns; verify the location yourself before paying.
Prize costs and novelty fade: last season's popular plush stops selling tries.
Theft, coin-box break-ins and vandalism in unattended spots.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Call your local licensing office and ask how crane games and prizes are classed where you are.
Visit existing machines nearby at busy times and watch how many people play.
Ask three venue managers whether they would host a machine and on what split.
Price a used machine, a card reader and a first batch of prizes.
Work out the tries per week needed to cover prizes and the host's share; drop the idea if that looks unlikely for the spot.
Get any licence or permit the machine needs and register the business.
Sign the location agreement before buying, then place one machine.
Set payout within local rules and write down the settings.
Log tries, prize cost and takings each visit.
Rotate prizes based on what gets played, and add a second machine only once the first covers its costs.

faq.a: It depends on where you are. Many places treat them as amusement games of skill, while others have classed some cranes as games of chance, capped prize values or banned them. Ask your local licensing authority before you buy a machine.

faq.q: Can I adjust how often a claw machine wins?
faq.a: Most machines allow it, but some places regulate payout and prize value, and players notice machines that feel impossible. Keep settings within local rules and record them.

faq.q: Is a small arcade better than single machines?
faq.a: An arcade spot gives you more machines under one roof but adds rent, staff hours and fit-out costs. Most people test with one or two machines in someone else's venue first.
